parts.visual:
When a founder takes their company public, they usually lose control to the Board of Directors. A 'Dual-Class Stock Structure' is how a founder prevents this and remains a corporate dictator.

The Structure:
1. Class A Shares: Sold to the public. 1 Share = 1 Vote.
2. Class B Shares: Kept exclusively by the founder. 1 Share = 10 Votes.

Result: The founder can own only 15% of the company's financial equity, but hold 51% of the voting power. They cannot be fired.
parts.audio: A Dual-Class Stock Structure allows a founder to keep control of a public company. By giving themselves 'Super-Voting' shares, the founder cannot be fired, even if they own less than 50% of the company.

questions.question: Mark Zuckerberg owns less than 15% of Meta's total stock, but he controls over 50% of the voting power. How is this legally possible?
options: He instituted a Dual-Class Stock Structure during the IPO. His personal 'Class B' shares carry 10x the voting power of the 'Class A' shares sold to regular investors.
questions.correct_answer: He instituted a Dual-Class Stock Structure during the IPO. His personal 'Class B' shares carry 10x the voting power of the 'Class A' shares sold to regular investors.
questions.explanation: This means that even if every single other shareholder in the world votes to fire him, his vote overrules all of them combined.

questions.question: Listen to the enraged Activist Investor. What is their complaint?
questions.tts_text: This company is essentially a monarchy. We provided 80% of the capital to fund the business, but we have zero legal power to replace the management.
options: The inherent unfairness of the Dual-Class structure, which separates financial risk from voting control.
questions.correct_answer: The inherent unfairness of the Dual-Class structure, which separates financial risk from voting control.
questions.explanation: Wall Street hates dual-class structures because it neuters their power, but they accept it if the founder is a genius who makes them money.

questions.question: Why do visionary founders fight so hard to establish a Dual-Class structure before an IPO?
options: To protect the long-term vision of the company from Wall Street analysts who only care about short-term, 90-day profits.
questions.correct_answer: To protect the long-term vision of the company from Wall Street analysts who only care about short-term, 90-day profits.
questions.explanation: Founders want to build 10-year projects (like the Metaverse). Wall Street hates 10-year projects. The founder uses super-voting shares to protect the vision.

questions.question: What is a 'Sunset Clause' in a Dual-Class structure?
options: A legally binding agreement that the 'Super-Voting' power will automatically expire after a certain number of years (e.g., 7 years), returning the company to a standard 1-share-1-vote democracy.
questions.correct_answer: A legally binding agreement that the 'Super-Voting' power will automatically expire after a certain number of years (e.g., 7 years), returning the company to a standard 1-share-1-vote democracy.
questions.explanation: This is a compromise to appease Wall Street, ensuring the founder doesn't act as a dictator forever.
